title: Hiring manager, mid data and ML, strong answers

questions.text: Walk me through the most important model or analysis you shipped in the last two years.
Tell me about a time you had to choose between a better model and faster delivery.
Why are you looking to move now, and why this role?
How do you work with engineers and product partners?
Tell me about a project that crossed team lines.
Where have you changed your mind about how to do data work?

persona.pushback_style: asks what would change the decision

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Ravi, welcome. I'm Helen, I lead the data science group. We have forty five minutes, and I want to understand your experience and what you want next.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thanks Helen. I've been looking forward to this conversation.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Where are you joining from today?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: From home in the north of the city. It has been a rainy week, so I'm glad to be inside.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. I'll ask about three or four pieces of your work and your reasons for the move, and we will keep time at the end for you.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Walk me through the most important model or analysis you shipped in the last two years.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Last year I led the churn prediction model for the subscription product at Alder and Finch, a mid size retailer. Before that, retention emails went to everyone. I built a gradient boosted model on 14 months of usage data, and I spent two weeks on the label definition because my first one leaked future data. In a holdout test, targeted emails lifted retention by 3.1 points and cut email volume by 40 percent. I ran the test and presented it to finance.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide the model was good enough to ship?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I set the bar before training. The retention team could only contact 10 percent of users, so I needed precision above 35 percent in the top decile. The model reached 41 percent. A logistic regression got 33, so I chose the boosted model despite the harder explanation, and I added feature importance reports so the team could trust it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a time you had to choose between a better model and faster delivery.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: On a demand forecasting project, a deep model beat our baseline by 6 percent in error, but it needed a new serving setup that would take eight weeks. I proposed shipping the simpler model in three weeks and keeping the deep one for later. I showed the planners that the gain was worth about 40 thousand dollars a quarter, which was not enough to wait. We shipped the simple one, and I wrote down what would make us revisit the choice. Two quarters later that threshold was met.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What if the planners had pushed for the better model?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would have asked what decision the extra accuracy changes. If they could show it changes an order size, I would have put the deep model first. In this case their own numbers said it did not, so we agreed.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why are you looking to move now, and why this role?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I grew our forecasting work from one analyst to a team of four, and I mentored two of them. Now I want to work on problems where the model drives a product decision directly, not only a report. Your posting mentions ranking and personalization, which is the area I have shipped in twice. I also want a larger scope, with two or three projects running at once.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a project that crossed team lines.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Last spring I worked with the platform team, the pricing team and legal on a data retention change. Our features depended on logs that would be deleted after 90 days. I wrote a one page proposal with the cost of each option, and I ran two meetings to agree on a 180 day window for hashed data. It kept 11 of our 14 features running and passed legal review in three weeks.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thank you. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How does the team decide which models go to production, and who owns them after launch?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: The model owner decides with a review from one peer and one engineer. The owner stays on call for the model for the first quarter, then it moves to a shared rotation.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That is all the time we have. Thanks Ravi, we will be in touch within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Helen. I enjoyed it.

notes: Strong for mid: own role, numbers and trade-offs in every answer.
